extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, policymakers, and legal professionals researching the News of the World phone-hacking scandal
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article-style summary of the News of the World phone-hacking scandal, its investigations, legal proceedings, inquiries, ethical critiques, and wider political and regulatory consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with criminal law and PCC code of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our journalists work within the criminal law and the Press Complaints Commission code of conduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by publishers (e.g., Trinity Mirror) to reject allegations; functions as an explicit defense/standard invoked by media organizations. The article contrasts this claim with allegations and evidence that suggest illegal acts occurred despite such assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial maxim: 'Get it first. But, first, get it right.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalistic maxim cited: "Get it first. But, first, get it right," which speaks for accurate reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes accuracy over speed; the article notes that this maxim supports accurate reporting but does not address the ethics or legality of how information was obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on illegal access to communications
rubrics_metrics.description: "It's wrong. It's not a grey area. What they did was illegal and, even if it weren't, it's just plain wrong. There's no defence for it. Even the government needs a warrant to get into a house or a computer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed by journalism academics/commentators (e.g., Stephen B. Shepard) as a categorical ethical and legal standard: journalists must not obtain information by illegal intrusion into voicemails/computers; privacy and warrant requirements are invoked as benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leveson Inquiry remit: scope for public inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveson was named to chair an inquiry "with a remit to look into the specific claims about phone hacking at the News of the World, the initial police inquiry and allegations of illicit payments to police, and a second inquiry to review the general culture and ethics of the British media."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines what a public judicial inquiry should examine: specific wrongdoing, institutional investigations, possible corruption (payments to police), and broader media culture and ethics; also indicates inclusion of broadcasters and social media in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of legal/advisory scope and client confidentiality (Harbottle & Lewis)
rubrics_metrics.description: H&L stated it "provided very narrow advice on whether the emails in question could be used to support Clive Goodman's allegations..." and that "the terms of their contract with NI explicitly stated that their advice should not be disclosed to a third party without H&L's written consent" and they "could not have reported NI to the police... because of client confidentiality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets a standard for interpreting legal advice: external legal opinions are limited by their contractual scope and confidentiality obligations, cannot serve as broad public 'good conduct certificates', and may not trigger reporting to authorities absent waivers or other steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator investigatory standard (Solicitors Regulation Authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: "On the basis of our preliminary review of the public domain material, we have decided to instigate a formal investigation. We will pursue our investigation vigorously and thoroughly, but emphasise that our inquiries are at an early stage, and that no conclusions have been reached about whether there may have been any impropriety by any solicitor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the SRA's threshold and procedural posture for opening formal investigations: preliminary public-material review, vigorous inquiry, and withholding conclusions until investigation is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct legal interpretation for interception offences
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records criticism that the CPS told police that "phone hacking was only an offence if messages had been intercepted before they were listened to by the intended recipient;" which a committee found to be incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals a legal-standard criterion: accurate statutory and case-law interpretation is essential to proper criminal investigation and prosecution; incorrect legal advice can hinder enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness in examination and prosecution of gathered evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most of the evidence obtained during these investigations remained unevaluated at Scotland Yard for ten years."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicates a procedural/quality standard for police investigations: evidence should be promptly and properly examined; long delays can prevent accountability and allow systemic issues to persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of gossip, sensationalism, and manufactured controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that some News Corporation papers replaced "responsible journalism with 'gossip, sensationalism, and manufactured controversy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions as an editorial quality criterion: journalism should prioritize responsible reporting over sensationalism; manufactured controversy undermines journalistic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory balance: concerns about state regulation vs self-regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records anxieties that a government inquiry or new regulation might threaten a free press, and debates whether stronger state regulation or stricter enforcement/self-regulation better address abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames a policy-evaluation criterion: regulatory responses must balance protection of individual privacy and accountability with preserving press freedom; the effectiveness of state vs self-regulation is a central metric in assessing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate cultural responsibility for newsroom practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary describing a culture where "you do whatever it takes to get the story, take no prisoners, destroy the competition, and the end will justify the means," and that leadership "encouraged lawbreaking and hacking phones and condoned it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates media organizations on culture and leadership: newsroom incentives, leadership behavior, and corporate norms are criteria for whether unethical or illegal practices are systemic or isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints and procedures for evidence sharing by retained advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: H&L said it had asked News International to release them from their professional duty of confidentiality, which had been declined; later News International authorised H&L to answer questions from police and parliamentary select committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies a procedural standard for converting private legal work into usable public evidence: waivers or authorizations are necessary to allow solicitors to disclose information to investigators or parliamentary bodies; without such waivers, disclosure is constrained.
